opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think it's usually malicious. Mostly it comes down to where the effort goes.

When you're developing your own method, you spend months on it. You tune the learning rate and the architecture, and you try a dozen tricks until something works. Every time it underperforms, you dig in and figure out why, because you're motivated to make it succeed.

Then you need a baseline, and you grab some existing implementation. Maybe you run it with the default hyperparameters from a paper that used a different setup. You run it once, it gives you a number, and that number goes in the table. Nobody spends three weeks debugging the baseline. If it does badly, that's a bit convenient, so there's no pressure to ask whether something went wrong.

There are a few specific ways this shows up:

- **Hyperparameter tuning asymmetry.** Your method gets a big sweep and the baseline gets one or two configurations. Even with a fair-looking sweep, you probably designed the search space with your own method in mind.
- **Bugs that only get fixed in one direction.** If your method produces a weird result, you hunt for the bug. If the baseline does, you shrug. So the bugs that survive are disproportionately in the baselines.
- **Setup mismatch.** The baseline was designed for a different environment, compute budget, or data regime, and you port it over without adapting it the way its authors would have.
- **Implementation details.** In deep learning, and especially deep RL, small things like normalization, reward scaling, or initialization can matter enormously. A from-scratch reimplementation often misses some of them.

There have been papers showing this pretty directly. When people carefully re-tune older methods, a lot of the claimed progress shrinks or vanishes. Well-tuned simple baselines often turn out to be competitive with fancier methods.

So I think of it as a structural incentive problem more than an individual integrity problem. The fix is mostly cultural and procedural: give baselines the same tuning budget, use the original authors' code where possible, and as a reviewer, ask whether the baseline numbers match what's been reported elsewhere.

r001.rationale: The response explains that baselines often get only default settings or one or two configurations while the new method receives extensive tuning, which can leave the baseline performing worse than it could.

fable-5.1.text:
Rohin Shah: Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's mostly not deliberate. There's a pretty strong selection effect going on. If you're developing a new method, you're spending months thinking about it, tuning the hyperparameters, debugging weird failure modes, noticing when the learning rate is slightly off. And then for the baseline, you spend maybe an afternoon. You grab whatever implementation is lying around, you use whatever hyperparameters were in the original paper, which were tuned for a different environment, and you run it once.

And the thing is, if the baseline underperforms, that's good news for you. So there's no pressure to go back and check whether you did something wrong. Whereas if your own method underperforms, you dig in, you find the bug, you fix it. So you end up with this asymmetry where your method has been debugged much more thoroughly than the thing you're comparing against. Nobody has to be acting in bad faith for that to happen. It's just where the incentives point.

There's also a more subtle version, which is that people often don't realize how much of the performance of a method comes from implementation details that aren't in the paper. In deep RL especially, things like reward normalization, observation clipping, how you handle the end of an episode, these can matter as much as the algorithmic idea. So you reimplement the baseline "faithfully" according to the paper and it just doesn't work as well, because the original authors had a bunch of tricks that they didn't think were worth mentioning.

And then I think the third thing is that people sometimes compare against a baseline that was never really designed for the setting they're testing in. Like, "we evaluated on this new benchmark, and the standard method does badly." Well, sure, but nobody ever tried to make the standard method work there. If someone spent the same effort on it, it might be fine.

So when I read papers, I tend to pay a lot more attention to whether the authors seem to have genuinely tried to make the baseline work. If the paper says "we did a hyperparameter sweep for both methods," or they match published numbers on the original benchmark before moving to the new one, I'm much more inclined to believe the result. If the baseline numbers are just way below what the original paper reported, that's usually a sign that something went wrong, and it's not the baseline's fault.

r001.rationale: It says the baseline gets little tuning and may use hyperparameters tuned for a different environment, which can make it underperform.

astra-6.text:
Often it’s just that you spend much more time getting your own method to work than you spend getting the baseline to work. You try your method, it doesn’t work, and you think, “Well, there must be a bug,” or, “Maybe these hyperparameters are wrong.” And you keep investigating until it does work. Whereas if the baseline doesn’t work, that fits your expectation that your method is better, so you’re more likely to accept that result.

You don’t have to be deliberately doing anything misleading. You just have a much stronger incentive to understand what’s going wrong with your own method. And things like hyperparameter tuning, or seemingly minor implementation choices, can make a pretty substantial difference. So you can end up comparing a very carefully tuned version of your method against a baseline that hasn’t received the same attention.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers spend less effort getting a baseline to work and may accept its poor result, while hyperparameter tuning can substantially affect performance. It explicitly describes comparing a carefully tuned method with an under-attended baseline.

sol-6.1.text:
I think usually it’s pretty mundane. You have some new idea, and you spend a lot of time getting it to work. You tune the hyperparameters, you debug it, you develop an intuition for when it’s doing the right thing. And then you need a baseline to compare against, so you take an existing implementation and run it with the default settings. But those settings might have been chosen for a different problem, and the baseline might need just as much tuning as your method did.

There’s also an asymmetry in how you respond to results. If your method performs badly, you think, “There must be a bug,” and you investigate. If the baseline performs badly, well, that’s what you were expecting — that’s why you’re proposing a new method. So you’re less likely to notice that you’ve implemented something incorrectly or given it an unsuitable configuration. You can end up with a comparison that looks quite convincing without anyone deliberately trying to make it unfair.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers often run a baseline with default settings chosen for a different problem, even though it may need tuning too, which can make it perform worse than it could.
